Reverse transcriptase is the enzyme that converts HIV's RNA into DNA; then, the enzyme integrase inserts HIV's genetic material into the host cell's genome

The DNA inserted into the host cell (the infected cell) is called a provirus. The host cell contains an enzyme called DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which is responsible of reading the DNA and creating RNA from it (this is called transcription). The host cell's DNA-dependent RNA polymerase reads the provirus and creates HIV's RNA which is required for creating more copies of the virus.

Gaming is going to be the most demanding task on your computer. You've already mentioned wanting to run Steam on Linux:

Why not run the Steam OS

The SteamOS website lists:

  • required disk space
  • required processor
  • required video card
  • minimum RAM

Once you get it installed, it's a tricked-out Debian-based system that meets the specs for a Steam Box.

From there you can just install whatever extra apps you need to get your work done, java, text-editor of choice, etc.

Give Manjaro Linux a try. It's an Arch based distro that's doesn't require you to use CLI to install it. You can boot into a live environment and install it from there. The process is quite simple, even setting up the partitions and such, no cfdisk or fdisk or cgdisk or whatever.

Since it's an Arch based distro you will get access to Arch User Repository which is pretty cool and has I believe every available Linux package. Steam and video games work fine, I run it on AMD 7790 and Catalyst with no issues so far.

But the best thing about Manjaro is that it's a rolling release distro, just like Arch. That means that every week or so you will get regular updates with the latest software. Now, many people argue that rolling release model is not okay if you're looking for a super stable system. From my experience and frustration of dealing with such people I can only say that those people don't know jack shit and need to shut the fuck up already and go back to their dependency web clusterfucks that won't even let me properly compile my own kernel. Sorry about the rant there. It's just that the system runs smooth as long as you use # pacman -Syyu and don't go into Octopi update adventure.

But if you really want to go balls deep in Linux, go the hardest way. Learn to build your own Linux From Scratch and spice it up with Gentoo on a second machine. The learning curve is very steep, but you'll grow an awesome beard and your girlfriend will leave you for an Ubuntu user.

The kernel is were the magic is. No matter what distribution you use, if you know how to really use CLI then they are all similar. Once you reach that point it's more like "I use Linux", instead of just a specific distro. I suggest using CLI for as much as you can, even just simple updates and installs. Then look up some resources on bash scripting. You'll be very pleased with the whole new world. To reiterate, Linux is not about the GUI, the real magic is in the command line.

I know it's late and you've already "decided," but here's my input since most Linux users change things as fast as they change their underwear... which can be pretty gross or hygienic, depending on the user-type you envision, and both are pretty correct.

I wouldn't recommend Ubuntu for multiple reasons, one being the Amazon "adware" on your Unity Desktop and Unity itself, but if you're going to do the Ubuntu thing, I'd create numerous partitions.

First, create one for your /home directory... and this will make sense in a minute.

Next, create your swap partition (argumentative area, but I like to do twice the amount of RAM as a good rule-of-thumb).

Finally, halve the rest of your HD space. One of these will go with your _buntu distro (again, I'd stay away from Ubuntu and try a flavor -- maybe Xubuntu or Kubuntu, depending on what kind of system you have... but I'd recommend Mint). The other half will go to your "DEEP" Linux distro... I'd recommend Arch.

Now, since you have a separate partition for your /home directory, all of your personal files should be available to both distros, regardless of which one you boot into. This way, you can use your main distro (again, preferably Mint) as an every-day distro and you can use your "DEEP" distro to learn.

Partitioning sizing will be dependent on how big your HD is, and how much RAM you have.
